blocks.text: Random projection takes high-dimensional vectors, often hundreds or thousands of dimensions, and maps them down to a much smaller number of dimensions using a random matrix, while approximately preserving the pairwise distances between points, a surprising guarantee that makes it a fast, simple tool for speeding up nearest neighbor search over large embedding collections.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. The Curse of Dimensionality

As the number of dimensions grows, distance calculations become more expensive, memory usage grows, and many nearest neighbor search structures lose their effectiveness, a set of problems collectively known as the curse of dimensionality. Reducing dimensionality before search is a common, practical way to fight back against these costs.

Search structures like the space partitioning trees from earlier in this module tend to degrade toward scanning almost every point as dimensionality grows, since in very high dimensions, distances between all pairs of points start to look similar, and pruning branches becomes far less effective.

blocks.title: A concrete symptom
blocks.content: In two or three dimensions, nearest neighbor search is fast and intuitive, but at a thousand dimensions, nearly every pair of points can end up almost equally distant, making it hard for any index structure to prune away irrelevant candidates.

blocks.text: 2. What a Random Projection Is

A random projection multiplies a high-dimensional vector by a random matrix whose entries are drawn from a simple distribution, typically standard Gaussian, producing a new, lower-dimensional vector, no learning or data-dependent fitting is involved, the matrix is generated once, randomly, and reused for every vector.

code.content:
import numpy as np
original_dim, target_dim = 768, 64
random_matrix = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=(original_dim, target_dim)) / np.sqrt(target_dim)
vector = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=original_dim)
projected = vector @ random_matrix
print(projected.shape)   # (64,)

blocks.title: No training needed
blocks.content: Unlike PCA or a learned embedding model, a random projection matrix requires zero training data and zero fitting time, it can be generated in a single line before any vectors even exist.

blocks.text: 3. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma

The Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma is the mathematical guarantee behind random projection, it states that a set of points in high-dimensional space can be projected into a much lower-dimensional space such that pairwise distances are preserved up to a small, controllable distortion, and remarkably, the required target dimension depends only on the number of points and the allowed distortion, not on the original dimensionality at all.

blocks.title: The surprising part
blocks.content: A collection of a million points can often be safely projected down to just a few hundred dimensions, regardless of whether the original vectors had one thousand or one hundred thousand dimensions.

blocks.text: The lemma was originally proved in the context of embedding metric spaces into low-dimensional Euclidean space, and it has since become one of the most widely used tools in randomized algorithms, machine learning, and large-scale search systems.

The lemma is a distortion guarantee, not an exact preservation guarantee, distances after projection are only guaranteed to fall within a factor of one plus or minus epsilon of their original values, never exactly equal.
4. How Much Distortion to Expect

The Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma gives a formula relating the target dimension, the number of points, and an allowed distortion factor epsilon, smaller epsilon, tighter distance preservation, requires a larger target dimension, while a looser epsilon allows a smaller target dimension at the cost of more approximate distances.
5. Why Random Works

A random matrix with independent, zero-mean entries tends to spread out and preserve the geometric relationships between vectors on average, because the inner product between a fixed vector and a random direction concentrates tightly around its expected value as the number of random directions grows, this concentration phenomenon is the deep reason a random, rather than carefully learned, projection can still preserve distances so reliably.

This concentration effect is closely related to the concentration of measure phenomenon, a broader idea in high-dimensional probability stating that many quantities computed from many independent random pieces tend to cluster tightly around their average value, rather than spreading out widely.

This is the same underlying phenomenon, applied from a different angle, as the concentration inequalities that show up in probability theory whenever many independent random contributions are averaged together.
6. Building a Random Projection Matrix

A basic random projection matrix draws each entry independently from a Gaussian distribution with mean zero, then scales the whole matrix by one over the square root of the target dimension, this scaling keeps the expected length of a projected vector close to the expected length of the original vector.

code.content:
from sklearn.random_projection import GaussianRandomProjection

transformer = GaussianRandomProjection(n_components=128, random_state=42)
reduced = transformer.fit_transform(high_dim_vectors)   # (n_samples, 128)

# verifying the scaling keeps expected vector length stable
import numpy as np
R = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=(768, 64)) / np.sqrt(64)
v = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=768)
print(np.linalg.norm(v), np.linalg.norm(v @ R))   # roughly comparable magnitudes

blocks.text: Most machine learning libraries, including scikit-learn, provide a ready-made random projection transformer, so in practice a team rarely needs to hand-generate and manage the random matrix directly.
7. Sparse Random Projections

A sparse random projection matrix replaces most entries with exact zeros, keeping only a small fraction non-zero, this variant is much faster to apply and store while still satisfying a version of the Johnson-Lindenstrauss guarantee, making it especially attractive when the original dimensionality is extremely large.

blocks.text: The very sparse variant, sometimes using only a fraction of a percent non-zero entries, was specifically designed for text data with extremely large vocabulary-sized dimensions, where a dense random matrix would be too large to even store in memory.
8. Random Projection vs PCA

Principal component analysis, the dimensionality reduction technique from the eigendecomposition lesson in the Linear Algebra module, learns a data-dependent projection that maximizes preserved variance, while random projection uses no data at all, just randomness. Random projection is far cheaper to compute, since it requires no eigendecomposition, and works well when only approximate distance preservation is needed, while PCA gives a tighter, data-optimized reduction at a higher computational cost.

items: Random projection: no data needed, extremely fast, slightly looser distance preservation guarantee.
PCA: requires the full dataset upfront, more expensive to compute, but gives the tightest possible variance-preserving reduction for that specific dataset.
A hybrid approach some systems use: random projection first to shrink dimensionality cheaply, then PCA on the smaller result for a final, refined reduction.

blocks.text: 9. Preserving Angles and Cosine Similarity

Random projection preserves not just Euclidean distances but also, approximately, the angles between vectors, which means cosine similarity, the standard similarity measure used throughout the similarity and distance metrics module, survives the projection nearly intact, making random projection a safe preprocessing step even for cosine-based nearest neighbor search.

This angle-preservation property follows from the same underlying inner-product concentration argument that preserves Euclidean distance, since cosine similarity is itself just a normalized inner product.
10. Computational Cost

Applying a dense random projection to a single vector costs time proportional to the original dimension times the target dimension, a single matrix multiply, which is typically far cheaper than the cost of building and querying an exact nearest neighbor structure directly in the original high-dimensional space, especially once the collection has millions of vectors.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Cost"],"rows":[["Build random matrix once","original dimension times target dimension"],["Project one vector","original dimension times target dimension"],["Project a batch of n vectors","n times original dimension times target dimension"]]}

blocks.title: Amortized cost
blocks.content: The one-time cost of generating the random matrix is paid once, while every subsequent vector projected through that same matrix pays only the much smaller per-vector multiplication cost.

blocks.text: 11. Locality-Sensitive Hashing Connection

Random projections are also the mathematical basis of one major family of locality-sensitive hashing, where the sign of the projection onto several random directions is used to assign a compact hash code to each vector, this connects random projection directly to the hashing lesson later in this module, both rely on the same random-direction-preserves-similarity idea.

Specifically, this connects to the random hyperplane family of locality-sensitive hash functions, where each random direction contributes one bit to a hash code, and vectors with a small angle between them are likely to land on the same side of most random hyperplanes, producing the same hash bit.
12. Use in Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

In practice, random projection is often applied as a cheap preprocessing step before running an approximate nearest neighbor search structure, reducing a large embedding collection from, say, 1536 dimensions down to a few hundred can significantly speed up both the index build time and the query time, while distances remain close enough to the original space that the retrieved nearest neighbors are still highly accurate.

code.content:
reduced_query = transformer.transform(query_vector.reshape(1, -1))
# then run any nearest neighbor search on the much smaller reduced_query

blocks.title: A real pipeline
blocks.content: Embed documents at 1536 dimensions, random-project down to 256, build an approximate nearest neighbor index on the 256-dimensional vectors, then optionally re-rank the top candidates using the original full-precision embeddings for a final accuracy boost.

blocks.text: Many production vector databases expose random projection, or a closely related learned projection, as an optional preprocessing configuration precisely because of this speed and memory tradeoff.
13. Choosing the Target Dimension in Practice

While the Johnson-Lindenstrauss formula gives a theoretical bound, real systems usually pick the target dimension empirically, by measuring how much retrieval accuracy degrades at a few candidate dimensions and choosing the smallest one that keeps accuracy within an acceptable tolerance.

A common empirical protocol is to hold out a small validation set of queries with known true nearest neighbors, then sweep candidate target dimensions and measure recall at each one, picking the smallest dimension whose recall loss stays within an acceptable, predetermined tolerance.
14. A Worked Example
Project two 4-dimensional vectors down to 2 dimensions using a small random matrix and compare the distance before and after.

code.content:
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(0)
a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0])
b = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 4.0, 3.0])
original_dist = np.linalg.norm(a - b)

R = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=(4, 2)) / np.sqrt(2)
a_proj, b_proj = a @ R, b @ R
projected_dist = np.linalg.norm(a_proj - b_proj)
print(original_dist, projected_dist)   # roughly similar, not identical

blocks.text: Even in this tiny four-dimensional example, the projected distance is already a reasonable approximation of the original distance, and the approximation only gets statistically tighter as more dimensions and more random directions are involved.

code.content:
# same example, comparing relative error directly
rel_error = abs(float(projected_dist) - float(original_dist)) / float(original_dist)
print(rel_error)

blocks.text: 15. Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to scale the random matrix by one over the square root of the target dimension, which leaves projected vectors with the wrong expected length.
Using a target dimension far below the Johnson-Lindenstrauss recommendation and being surprised when nearest neighbor accuracy drops noticeably.
Regenerating a new random matrix for every batch of vectors, instead of fixing one matrix and reusing it, which breaks distance preservation between vectors projected at different times.
Assuming random projection improves accuracy, its purpose is speed and memory savings at the cost of a small, controlled amount of distortion, not better distances.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is projecting the query vector and the stored vectors with two different random matrices, distances are only meaningfully comparable when every vector, query included, passes through the exact same fixed projection matrix.

A sixth common mistake is confusing random projection with random sampling, random projection keeps every vector but shrinks its dimensionality, while random sampling keeps full vectors but throws away some of the data points entirely, the two solve entirely different problems.
16. Practice: Measure Distortion

Project a set of 100 random 500-dimensional vectors down to 50 dimensions, then compute the average relative difference between original and projected pairwise distances, and observe how that average distortion shrinks as the target dimension increases.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.random_projection import GaussianRandomProjection
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist

X = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=(100, 500))
original_dists = pdist(X)
reduced = GaussianRandomProjection(n_components=50, random_state=1).fit_transform(X)
reduced_dists = pdist(reduced)
distortion = np.abs(original_dists - reduced_dists) / original_dists
print(distortion.mean())

# extend: try target dimensions 10, 50, 100, 200 and plot mean distortion
for dim in [10, 50, 100, 200]:
    reduced = GaussianRandomProjection(n_components=dim, random_state=1).fit_transform(X)
    d = np.abs(original_dists - pdist(reduced)) / original_dists
    print(dim, d.mean())

blocks.text: A further extension worth trying is repeating the whole experiment with several different random seeds, confirming that the average distortion stays roughly consistent across different random matrices, since the guarantee is probabilistic, not a property of any single fixed random draw.
Key Takeaway

Random projection maps high-dimensional vectors into a much smaller space using a fixed random matrix, and the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma guarantees that pairwise distances survive this mapping up to a small, controllable distortion, with no data-dependent learning required at all.

This lesson opens the ANN Search Mathematics module, the same random-direction idea reappears in the hashing lesson next, where the sign of a random projection becomes a compact hash bit, and later in the space partitioning and quantization lessons that build the rest of the approximate nearest neighbor search toolkit.

The angle-preserving property covered in the newly added section means random projection is just as safe to use ahead of cosine-similarity-based search as it is ahead of Euclidean-distance-based search, covering both major distance families used throughout approximate nearest neighbor systems.

Because random projection needs no training data at all, it also works well as a first, cheap step in a streaming system where new vectors arrive continuously and there is no fixed dataset available upfront to fit a data-dependent method like PCA against.
